newsitem.title: USA: $6.5 million for U.S. campaign funds probe.
newsitem.headline: $6.5 million for U.S. campaign funds probe.

text.p: A divided Senate committee that will probe campaign finance abuses approved a $6.5 million budget on Thursday and expanded the investigation beyond the 1996 presidential election.

By a 9-to-7 vote on strictly party lines, the Republican-controlled Senate Governmental Affairs committee approved a Republican plan for a special investigation budget to hire some 80 staff and investigators and hold hearings.
By the same 9-7 margin, the committee rejected a Democratic alternative for a $1.8 million budget with promises to increase funding later if necessary.

Under Democratic prodding, however, the committee agreed without dissent to broaden the investigation beyond the 1996 presidential campaign and include congressional elections, misuse of charitable and tax-exempt organisations, promises of special access in return for donations and whether contributions by corporations and labour groups are truly independent, as required by law.

While the committee said it would investigate matters other than the presidential election financing, the spotlight is expected to focus on contributions to Democrats from foreigners or people with ties to foreign businesses.
The FBI, the House and the Federal Election Commission also are investigating news reports of improper financing during the federal elections last year.

Senate committee chairman Fred Thompson, a Tennessee Republican, in arguing for the full $6.5 million, said there was a wide scope to the investigation, mentioning news reports that people from 11 foreign countries had been cited directly or indirectly about questionable contributions.

He told reporters the foreign countries were Taiwan, India, Mexico, South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Hong Kong, China, Vietnam, Russia and Paraguay. He said the committee needed money to carry out a broad investigation that included sending investigators overseas.

The committee's senior Democrat, John Glenn of Ohio, argued that $6.5 million was "a large, precedent-setting budget" that was nearly the size in current dollars of the select Senate Watergate committee that probed the scandal that led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974.

"It is an excessive amount to spend on any open-ended inquiry," Glenn said, claiming the $6.5 million exceeded the combined budgets of committees that investigated the Whitewater land deal of President Clinton and his wife and the Iran-Contra scandal under President Ronald Reagan.
The committee's budget plans must be approved by the Senate Rules committee and also by the full Senate.

Senate Democratic Leader Thomas Daschle of South Dakota told reporters there could be a Senate floor fight over the funding and said Republicans did not have the needed 60 votes to close debate and bring the matter to a vote.
